subject_name: Social Security and Medicare Payroll Tax (FICA)
intro: The Social Security and Medicare payroll tax rates, the Social Security wage base, and how the Additional Medicare Tax works for high earners.
explanation:
## What FICA pays for

The Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) tax has two parts. One funds Social Security, formally the old-age, survivors, and disability insurance programs. The other funds Medicare's hospital insurance. Employees and employers each pay both, and each part has its own rate.

## The rates

Social Security tax is charged at {fact:us_fica_ss_rate} on the employee and at the same {fact:us_fica_ss_rate} on the employer. The Medicare tax rate is {fact:us_fica_medicare} for each. Employers withhold the employee's share from wages and pay their own share on top.

## Only Social Security has a wage base

Earnings above the wage base are not subject to Social Security tax. In {tax_year}, Social Security tax stops applying to earnings above {fact:us_fica_wage_base}, the wage base. Medicare tax has no cap, so every covered dollar of wages is subject to it.

## The Additional Medicare Tax

Wages above a threshold also bear an Additional Medicare Tax of {fact:us_fica_addl_rate}. Employers must start withholding it in the pay period when an employee's wages for the year pass {fact:us_fica_addl_employer}, and they continue until the end of the year. This applies whatever the employee's filing status, and there is no employer match.

On your own return, the threshold depends on filing status: {fact:us_fica_addl_joint} for married couples filing jointly, {fact:us_fica_addl_mfs} for married people filing separately, and {fact:us_fica_addl_employer} for everyone else. If you receive both wages and self-employment income, the wages count first, and your threshold is reduced by the wages for the self-employment calculation. You report the tax on Form 8959, and some people ask their employer to withhold extra or make estimated payments to cover it.

## Self-employed people pay both halves

People who work for themselves pay the Social Security and Medicare taxes as self-employment tax instead of through an employer, and the same wage base applies.
